In various ATP explorations of whether an implication A⊨B holds (Higman-Neumann, conjunctions X∧Y, …), we search for a proof, and for finite counter-models. For Austin implications (that hold in finite magmas and fail for infinite magmas) neither side can succeed, regardless of computational power. Sometimes we can find proofs of finite implications by adding the property that injectivity ⇔ surjectivity for some specific functions (left/right multiplications, squaring, …). But to prove the non-implication for infinite magmas we need to construct infinite counterexamples. Are there any classes of infinite counterexamples that can be explored automatically? AFAIK, linear models cannot be interesting since they can always be reduced to large finite fields?

Concrete questions: how can I refute by an infinite magma construction the following implications that hold in finite magmas?

  • (3 x=x◇x)∧(73 x = y ◇ (y ◇ (x ◇ y))) ⊨ (125 x = y ◇ ((y ◇ x) ◇ y)) ,
  • (42323216 x = y ◇ ((((y ◇ y) ◇ x) ◇ z) ◇ (((y ◇ y) ◇ y) ◇ z))) ⊨ (67953691 x = (y ◇ y) ◇ (y ◇ ((x ◇ z) ◇ (((y ◇ y) ◇ y) ◇ z))))

One way to look for such techniques is to look at how we found counterexamples to implications true for finite magmas. An obvious standout is the greedy approach, as automated by Daniel Weber. Another is checking free magmas by finding a complete rewriting system. I think there also were some translation invariant models, which might be automatable given some ansatz, though I don't know if anyone has automated them for infinite magmas.

I doubt it will help with your implications, but infinite dimensional linear models can be interesting even when finite dimensional linear models are not, and this avoids any model theory tricks. For an example of this in the main project, there are linear counterexamples to the implication 1117→24411117 \to 24411117→2441 (see #Equational > Outstanding equations, v1 @ 💬 ), even though this implication holds for finite magmas.

Thanks @Matthew Bolan. Indeed, infinite-dimensional linear models don't reduce to finite models, I hadn't realized that. Regarding Daniel Weber's code in equational_theories/Generated/Greedy/src/forcer.py, I managed to run it but haven't yet decoded what its output (like [Rule([[0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 3]], [2, 3]), Rule([[0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 3]], [3, 0, 1]), Rule([[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 2]], [0, 2, 0])]) means. Maybe I can get away with using the whole pipeline all the way to Lean without understanding the intermediate steps precisely.

@Bruno Le Floch If I recall correctly, Rule([[0, 1, 2], [0, 1, 3]], [2, 3]) means that if we have defined 0⋄1=20 \diamond 1 = 20⋄1=2 and 0⋄1=30 \diamond 1 = 30⋄1=3, then we must have 2=32 = 32=3. Rule([[0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 3]], [3, 0, 1]) means that if we have already defined 0⋄1=20\diamond 1 = 20⋄1=2 and 0⋄2=30 \diamond 2 = 30⋄2=3, then we must have 3⋄0=13 \diamond 0 = 13⋄0=1. Also its likely that this conversation should be moved to a separate thread.
4 messages were moved here from #Equational > Thoughts and impressions thread by Bruno Le Floch.
For reference, #Equational > Equation 65 -> left cancellability @ 💬 is a good starting point to read up on Daniel Weber's greedy construction automation. I don't think there is any documentation.

@Bruno Le Floch A reply to your question of last September in this thread: law 67953691 does not imply law 40. Vampire found the countermodel and CeTA certifies it. Universal algebra is not my field: I work on logic and AI-assisted proving. Please check the claim before trusting it.

Claim. Law 67953691 is x = (y ◇ y) ◇ (y ◇ ((x ◇ z) ◇ (((y ◇ y) ◇ y) ◇ z))). It does not imply x ◇ x = y ◇ y. Your proof of November 2024 settles the finite case. The law is therefore Austin-equivalent to Higman–Neumann and not equivalent. Terence Tao expected this answer in his report in the Higman–Neumann thread. The model here is of a different kind from his.

How it was found. Vampire found it, not me. It saturates within seconds in its default portfolio mode and reports CounterSatisfiable.

fof(law, axiom, ![X,Y,Z]: X = m(m(Y,Y),m(Y,m(m(X,Z),m(m(m(Y,Y),Y),Z))))).
fof(goal, conjecture, ![X,Y]: m(X,X) = m(Y,Y)).

vampire --mode casc -t 60 problem.p

Vampire 5.0.0, 5.0.1 and 5.1.0 all succeed. Vampire 4.9 times out on the same file. Most of the Higman–Neumann work dates from late 2024, before version 5.0.0 came out. The winning strategy uses LPO with -tgt full and -gtg exists_sym. Drop any of the three and the result is lost. The saturated set holds 71 unit equations over ◇ and six auxiliary function symbols. The six symbols name subterms of the law.

Check. A prover's word is not enough. LPO orients the 71 equations into a rewrite system. CeTA 3.9 certifies three facts: the system terminates, it is locally confluent, and c ◇ c and d ◇ d have distinct normal forms. A second certificate shows that the system entails the law. In short, the ground normal forms make an infinite magma that satisfies 67953691, and its squares are not constant. Four files are attached: the two CPF certificates, the rule list and the TPTP problem. Nothing is formalized in Lean.

Three limits remain. First, the same portfolio run, ten minutes per law, finds nothing for the other 20 finite-equivalent laws or for the 13 unknown ones. Second, the rewrite system is all I know of the model. Third, Claude (Claude Code) did most of the setup, the runs and the checks. I answer for the claim. The credit for the model goes to Vampire.

If this is known or wrong, please say so. If it is useful, I can share the rest and help with a Lean version.

Attachments: 67953691_disproof.cpf.xml · 67953691_law.cpf.xml · 67953691_rules.txt · 67953691.p

Can't speak to whether or not it's known, but it checks out!

Because it's much easier to compress something than to find it in the first place, I was able to :robot: it down to a simpler decoder model. The constructoin is the free magma + one extra rule, where if the two inputs look like the outermost pieces of the RHS, then we return (after inverting) x.

I've been able to apply related decoder approaches to generate Lean proofs of non-HN-ness for 67953691, 67953597, 89177565, 129416953, 129420890, at least some of which were open at one point.

As far as I know the "state of the art" was up to date on the ETP repo at https://github.com/teorth/equational_theories/blob/main/data/Higman-Neumann.json and all the equations you listed were known to be equivalent to Higman-Neumann for finite magmas, but unknown for infinite. I'm a bit surprised to see in that file that none of the equations were known to have infinite countermodels.

A correction to my message above: Vampire 4.9 does not time out on this law, its portfolio mode does. Bisecting 4.9 to 5.0.0, the first commit where the winning strategy succeeds is PR #636 (18 December 2024). It only changes the default of -drc from the ordering check to encompassment demodulation (Duarte and Korovin, IJCAR 2022). With -drc encompass added, 4.9 finds the model in about 10 ms. With -drc ordering, 5.1.0 fails. The model needs LPO, -tgt full, -gtg exists_sym and -drc encompass together, a strategy that only entered the CASC 2025 schedule. So it was within reach in late 2024, with four options. I do not know why encompassment makes the saturation finite. Claude Code ran the bisection. Logs on request.

Update: 67953597, 67953691, 73285871, 73288447, 89177565, 129416953, 129420890, 48217520, 48217671 all have infinite non-HN models.

163876110 actually implies HN, thanks to Aristotle + Vampire, which is possibly the first non-counterexample result I've come across in the entire extended ETP. :upside_down:
